## Overview

Each year the Royal Statistical Society invites nominations for its Sports Statistic of the Year award. In this episode, Rich and Jess work through the 2025 shortlist, debating which entries best combine sporting insight with statistical clarity. They discuss how to judge a good sports statistic — from surprising findings to careful framing of uncertainty — and reflect on what the Corridor of Uncertainty might nominate in future years.

## Key Concepts

::: {.callout-tip}
## What Makes a Good Sports Statistic?
A compelling sports statistic should be surprising yet interpretable, grounded in reproducible data, and honest about limitations. The best entries tell a story about the sport while teaching the audience something about measurement and uncertainty.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Communicating Uncertainty
Sports statistics are often shared without confidence intervals, sample sizes, or definitions. The RSS award highlights examples that do this well — or cases where missing context leads to misleading conclusions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Public Engagement with Statistics
Awards like this help bridge academic statistics and everyday sports discourse, encouraging fans and journalists to think more critically about the numbers behind headlines.
:::

## Transcript Highlights

> "It's not just about the biggest number — it's about whether the stat actually changes how you understand the game."

The hosts emphasise that impact and clarity matter more than shock value alone when judging nominated statistics.

***

> "If you don't say what the denominator is, you've basically just written a headline."

A recurring theme is the importance of sample size, definitions, and context when sharing sports data publicly.

## Discussion

This episode sits at the intersection of sports analytics and statistical literacy. By walking through real shortlisted entries, Rich and Jess model how to critique sports statistics constructively — asking where data came from, what assumptions were made, and whether the conclusion follows from the evidence. The discussion complements more technical episodes on modelling and prediction by focusing on how results are communicated to a general audience.
